anomaly_def.Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and dead index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup workers can reclaim them.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes sustain near-saturation CPU consumption, starving other work and inflating latency.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, or thread counts, causing allocation failures.

When all three root causes are active, the system shows a compound failure signature: vacuum or purge workers spin at 100 % CPU yet make little progress, overall host load and context-switch rates soar, and the engine begins to log errors about failing to spawn new workers, open files, or extend shared memory. Query latencies rise non-linearly; some sessions stall on visibility checks of bloated tables while others are rejected outright by the kernel. Monitoring views show both a growing version store and a backlog of blocked or aborted background jobs. Administrators may observe that even emergency maintenance commands refuse to start because required handles or processes cannot be created.

Causal chain: heavy UPDATE/DELETE churn inflates the version store, awakening more cleanup workers; these workers consume additional CPU cycles and create more kernel objects (threads, file handles, async-I/O contexts). The extra CPU demand pushes the host to saturation, lengthening task-switch queues and slowing all workers—including those needed for cleanup—so the MVCC bloat worsens. Meanwhile, the multiplication of worker threads and open files drives the process toward OS resource ceilings; once those limits are reached, new vacuum workers and client sessions fail to start, eliminating the very mechanisms that could relieve version pressure. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another: MVCC bloat triggers CPU saturation, CPU saturation accelerates kernel object creation, OS denials block remediation, and the feedback loop rapidly degrades overall database availability.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the number of TCP keepalive messages that can be lost before the server connection to the client is considered dead.
entry.trigger_condition: The number of lost TCP keepalive probes reaches tcp_keepalives_count on systems supporting TCP_KEEPCNT.
entry.workload_impact: The server can consider the client connection dead after the configured keepalive failure threshold.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
